candidates.excerpt: More than two months after the Formula 1 race at Monza, the result has finally been confirmed. Audi believed that Racing Bulls driver Yuki Tsunoda – who was given the opportunity to stand in following Isack Hadjar's wrist injury and Liam Lawson's subsequent promotion – deserved a time penalty for a potential restart infringement. Following Charles Leclerc's heavy crash, there was a standing restart at the Temple of Speed, with Tsunoda initially heading towards the left side of the grid and therefore the wrong grid spot. After a late manoeuvre towards his actual grid spot, an extra formation lap followed. The sporting regulations stipulate that a driver who caused an extra formation lap must start from the end of the pitlane. Failure to do so could result in the offence being punished with a stop-and-go penalty. In Tsunoda's case, he started from the grid as normal, but the stewards decided to take no further action over the incident after the race.

If the same approach catches on elsewhere, you could tell an AI what you need, approve what it picks, and leave it to handle checkout.

The first one is NFS2ROOT, a heap buffer overflow vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s Network File System (NFS) server (nfsd), which allows threat actors to gain root privileges on a vulnerable Linux device remotely. The bug, now tracked as CVE-2026-99362, and was given a severity score of 9.8/10 (critical) was discovered by security researcher Jérémy Jean of ANSSI, who also submitted a fix in August 2026. But it being a critical-severity flaw is not the worst part - this bug has been hiding in the Linux kernel’s NFS server for 12 years. candidates.title: Rare rhino's first steps captured on video at zoo
candidates.excerpt: The moment a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros took its first steps at a zoo has been captured on video. The video shows 19-year-old mother Asha with her newborn calf at their enclosure after Asha had been pregnant for 15 months. Keepers said both rhinos were in good health and the birth was an important step in the conservation of the threatened species. Tom Garland from the rhino team at Chester Zoo said the calf was the fourth born to Asha and father Beni, who died earlier this year following a short and sudden illness. "It's always exciting to welcome a new calf and Asha has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters," he said. "Every birth is important for the future of this species and it's wonderful to see another healthy arrival." The species was driven to near-extinction in the early 1900s by habitat loss and trophy hunting and remains vulnerable to extinction with around 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos living in the wetlands, forests and grasslands of India and Nepal.
